R85.summary: Rome, 8 Jan 1567: the Pope wants to know whether the King's journey will go ahead, because he would then meet him wherever suits him; the Queen Mother and the King of France wish Philip to invite them to a parley; the Pope distrusts "words of women" but urges the King to admit, even seek, the meeting, leaving it to his prudence, and offers to act as common father.
R85.en:
His Holiness wishes to be made certain whether the King's journey will be for [3050], because, if so, he would wish to
meet the King in whatever place suits him best; which you will let the King know, telling him also that His Holiness
holds it as certain that the Queen [Mother] of France and His [French] Majesty desire that the King should ask them to
come to a parley with him, which they would do if asked. It is true that His Holiness says he does not know how far one
can build on women's words; but he begs and exhorts the King [3020] not to doubt that great fruit for the Catholic
religion may come of such a meeting, as […] is given to understand from several sides that great good will come of it
for religion, and that he should be willing to admit, nay to seek, such a meeting.

R86.summary: Rome, 25 July - 2 Aug 1567, Milan jurisdiction case: the Pope means, in confidence, to proceed with spiritual arms against the authors of the outrage, above all the Senate; the governor is to make them obey the monitories; the Holy See's dignity requires action at least against the Capitano di giustizia, the fiscal and some senators; the King should deprive his two ministers of office.
R86.en:
His Holiness's design, to tell it to Your Lordship alone without showing that you know it to others, is to proceed
against the authors of [?that] deed, and above all against the Senate, with his spiritual arms; and so he wants [?to
have] that order given as soon as possible to His Excellency [the governor of Milan] that he should, if need be, force
[them] to obey His Holiness's monitories whenever they are served on them; because there would truly be no dignity for
this Holy See unless one proceeded at least against the Capitano di giustizia and the fiscal, who has done the worst of
all, and against some of the Senate too, who, [2020] tainted with some notable vice, make more noise than the others, so
that they may not perhaps be punished for their sins, thinking by this [?way] to win all the more the King's favour;

R87.summary: About 2 Aug 1567: the Pope wants the King to go to Flanders soon, to restore religion there, in France and Germany; the Queen Mother of France wishes to be invited to a meeting, which the King should grant; the archbishop-elect of Cologne, unconfirmed and allied with the Duke of Cleves, is to be deprived, and the King should see that the chapter does not choose a suspect successor.
R87.en:
His Holiness wishes the King to go to Flanders as soon as possible, trusting in God that this journey of his must set
the world to rights and be a reform of all Christendom; and therefore he thinks that it will serve to restore religion
not only in that province but also in France and in Germany. His Holiness is given to understand that the Queen [Mother]
of France has a very great desire to be invited by the King to a meeting, from which it is believed great good and
profit could be drawn for Christendom, and that the King, who as far as is known seeks nothing but the service of God
and the public good, will obtain whatever he knows how to ask.

R88.summary: Rome, 4 Nov 1567, a chapter of a letter from France passed on to the nuncio: the Queen Mother is timid, trusts the Chancellor, Morvillier, Limoges and l'Aubespine, and keeps the kingdom divided to rule; not a Huguenot but a bad Christian; if the King imprisoned the Constable and his son until Condé and the Admiral laid down arms, the troubles would end.
R88.en:
As to the troubles of France, if the Queen [Mother] will act in earnest they will soon end, for one may reckon this a
fire of straw; but the Queen is so timid, and trusts so much in the Chancellor, in Morvillier, in Limoges and in
l'Aubespine, her counsellors, that she cannot resolve to do anything good, and keeps treating the evil with something
worse. And believe me, she does not sin from ignorance, for everything that has happened to her was foretold to her many
times; but there is so much ambition to rule in her that there is not as much in the whole world. And to tell you, the
Queen in my judgement is not a Huguenot, but I do believe she is a bad Christian, and that neither love nor charity nor
even justice reigns in her, letting herself be persuaded that keeping the kingdom divided is the true way to rule; and
how much she deceives herself anyone can easily see.

R89.summary: Second copy of the R88 text (the chapter of a letter on the Queen Mother and the French court), ending "da persona molto bene", continued in R90.
R89.en:

R90.summary: End of the same text: the writer is well informed of the French court and the Queen Mother; the King should let the Queen know that her counsellors, unfaithful to God, will be little faithful to her.
R90.en:
informed of the humours of that court and above all of the nature of the Queen [Mother]. It would perhaps be well for
the King to let the Queen know that she does not have those good counsellors about her whom she thinks she can trust,
because those who are unfaithful to God will be little faithful to her.
